item.title: Three Things at Thirty (for dudes)
item.description:
There’s two things I really wish I’d done much earlier in life, which I cannot catch-up with, due to the realities of aging. Also one thing I did do, which I’m happy about. So if you’re near 30, here’s three things you really should do ASAP.

1. Test Your T

As you age and your metabolism accrues errors, your hormone levels will degrade. Testosterone is the chemical of desire. As you lose it you’ll lose your motivation to do things in general, and attendant energy levels as well. Honestly, maybe this is a good thing? Maybe as we age we should set our sights lower and accept that we’ve won our biggest victories and cultivate the fruits of our prior accomplishments rather than striving for ever greater heights.

But maybe not. Maybe it’s good to stay hungry. The good news is that testosterone is super cheap to manufacture and very easy to supplement, so you can keep it at your healthy youthful levels indefinitely. The bad news is that by the time you realize you need it, you don’t know what those levels were.

Male testosterone ranges from 300 to 1,000 ng/dL (nanograms per deciliter). This is a very wide range! You probably want to aim to restore the level your healthy young body naturally produces and has adjusted to. But if you go in and test at 300 ng/dL there is no way for your doctor to know if your base level 10 years ago was 450 or 700 or 950. He’ll probably aim for a middle line, but that’s probably an under- or overshoot.

You can’t get this information from the past once it is the past. When you want it is when you can’t get it. Head this off. Go in and get your testosterone levels tested when you’re young so that when you get older you’ll know what to restore to.

Honestly you may want to do this in your late 20s. 30 is an easy-to-remember milestone though.

2. Finagle Some Finasteride

Finasteride prevents hair loss. With very few exceptions, men look better with a full head of hair. Keeping your hair is super easy, all you have to do is take Finasteride every day, which is readily available and cheap.

Unfortunately Finasteride doesn’t regrow hair (rare exceptions notwithstanding). You have to take it before you start losing your hair (or at the very first signs). The biggest difficulty with this is that no one EVER sees the top/back of their own head. Try it right now. I bet you can’t. Mirror doesn’t help, it shows you from the front. Even phone camera isn’t that useful because it’s hard to get a good angle by reaching back.

Your best option is to have a loved one you really trust enough to actually tell you when you’re starting to lose your hair, and to tell them that you want them to do that. If your partner will tell you when you have some food on your chin/teeth, they may be high-integrity enough to do this for you. Fortunately if you’re reading this you’re probably rat-adjacent so you likely have a partner that will do this for you. :) Otherwise you are basically doomed to not notice until at least a year past the time you should have started.

Again, this is a thing that you can’t get take-backs on. By the time you realize you need it, you’ve already suffered irrecoverable losses. So start early. At 30. Probably earlier tbh, many guys start losing hair before 30. But 30 is an easy-to-remember milestone.

Contrary to initial reports on finasteride, the chances of sexual dysfunction are extremely low — maybe 1%. And if you do experience them you can just stop finasteride and they go away. As a bonus, it may slightly slow down skin aging.

3. Suspend Your Spunk

If you’re like most career-minded moderns, your girlfriend/wife will start thinking about kids around 30. She’ll be ready for them around her early/mid-30s. At this point fertility is becoming hard. In America “Advanced Maternal Age” for a woman is 35 and hospitals generally treat her differently. If she’s been thinking ahead and has/had a career, she probably froze some eggs in her late 20s or early 30s. You may very well use these eggs to conceive.

This is a biologically intense process, and extremely expensive. You’re probably 2-4 years older than her, so if you haven’t planned ahead she’s using mid-30s to late-30s seed to fertilize a limited number of very expensive eggs. You’ve probably heard by now that male sperm quality also degrades with age. The sperm you make in your late 30s is worse than the sperm you made in your late 20s.

Your wife has gone through several intense medical procedures that cost her a ton of money to maximize the chance of healthy offspring. Getting your semen frozen is trivially easy and basically free in comparison. You’re paying maybe a thousand dollars the first time and $100-$200 a year to keep it in cryo storage. You should be willing to invest this minimal amount into your future children and to do your portion of the medical sexual effort.

Huge bonus - if you do this you can get a vasectomy without future regrets. This helps avoid some of the worst tail-risks of a condom failure, and opens up potential for less-protected sex with some close partners.

Honestly, younger sperm is better so you may want to do it even before 30. But 30 is an easy-to-remember milestone.

Timing

In all of these pre-30 is even better than 30. But in addition to being a milestone that’s easy to remember, pre-30 humans have more money constraints. These interventions are all pretty cheap in the grand scheme, but the practicalities of getting together a spare $1000 in your early 20s can be very daunting. By the time you’re 30 it still isn’t trivial, but at least now it’s not wrenchingly painful.

Of course the looming question over all this is “wtf are you talking about Eneasz. It’s almost 2027. Any advice that’s supposed to pay biological dividends years down the line is beyond irrelevant.”

OK. Yeah. It is weird to give this advice as if the age of classic biology wasn’t about to end, one way or another. I don’t know what the hell I’m doing either. Why write something like this when no one will care about their male pattern baldness soon either because they won't be alive to care or they won’t have to worry about it because they can choose any age and any body in any configuration?

But I dunno man. Maybe we get a pause. Maybe the Internet is harrowed. Maybe things limp along weirdly for another fifteen years and people still need to worry about their motivation levels and being attractive and having a small family to be happy with. In those timelines, I would have rather have been told these three things to do, than not.

There's nothing I can do*
item.description:
TL;DR: it seems to me that I am unable to do anything useful on the AI issue other than being informed. I feel bad about it.

Naive extrapolations point to extreme superintelligence in a year; I'll be 23 at that point. I keep reading about Really Trying and Getting Involved so that we hopefully don't die.

It is unclear to me that there's anything at all I can do in that regard.

Why I believe that:

  1. I am a 22yo undergraduate student at the only AI undergrad program in my country (Italy). I am not particularly technically or academically skilled, with Cs on average. I pass the class and move on.
  2. I have no money, as in, zero income at all; I can't move to London or the U.S.
  3. My country as a whole is not particularly influential or informed on the topic, and there is essentially no community around this. I may very realistically be one of 100-1,000 people in Italy who knows about the intellectual, forecasting and existential side of AI.
  4. Even the people at my own university (the literal only undergrads in Italy on AI) are stuck at GPT-4o levels. Anecdotally, they are not aware that AI can code at a professional level.

Here is what I am doing:

  1. I stay informed as much as possible. I regularly read LessWrong, Zvi, METR, Yudkowsky/Soares/CSET/others, as well as the various forecasts and proposals (AI 2027, AI 2040 and so on). Anything that seems useful to understand.
  2. I chat with people (as in, family and few friends/acquaintances) about AI, but it's not like they have much interest, and after a few minutes you've got to change the subject anyways.

That's it. I don't what else to do. Any way I spin it in my head, it appears to me that I am powerless to take any action.

I don't even want to work in AI. I already have career plans and goals in life, all of which are unrelated to AI. This post has been mostly hopeless, but I only feel that way about the current AI existential situation; things are otherwise going well.

I read 80,000 Hours' calls to use your career to help, and people's posts to get heavily involved... but I want to just go on with my life as planned. Maybe that's a fault in my character. I genuinely wonder.

Given the urgency and importance of the situation, I feel like I have to act; then I see the lineup of problems and constraints I have; then I think that if I really wanted to, I'd find a way; but I like my life the way it is, and I don't act. I feel a duty to help, and both huge obstacles against it and a lack of desire to do so. This makes me feel like a bad person. Perhaps it is an accurate assessment, perhaps it isn't.

I would like your opinion on this situation. There is no one else I can talk to about this.

item.title: Realize When You're Stupid
item.description:
[This post is the second post in my thirty day writing challenge. Tune in for more if you enjoy it!]

If you reliably knew that you would make a bad decision during a certain time, would you let yourself make decisions during that time? Probably not, right? So why do you let yourself grocery shop when hungry, speak negatively when you have low blood sugar, and make key decisions when anxious?

A core epistemic skill that I’ve tried to cultivate over the years is the idea of knowing when I’m stupid, and not letting myself make decisions during these times. Like all core epistemic skills, I’ve cultivated this in response to getting repeatedly smacked across the face over and over again.

I.

Cindy is an anxious woman. Her resting heart rate is a bit high, she gets wigged out easily, and she tends to run an endless stream of disaster loops through her head at all hours of the day. Like all anxious people, her anxiety rises and falls. Maybe it rises when her blood sugar is low, when she’s under-slept, or when other things in her life are particularly stressful. Probably all three.

She, like all people, has a number of decisions to make throughout the day. Some of these decisions are big and some of them are small. Cindy reliably finds that when she’s flooded with anxiety, she repeatedly runs into certain failure modes. For example, maybe she makes elaborate plans to fix every single problem in her entire life, half-commits to it for, like, one day, and then decides that: no, what was she thinking? That plan is terrible! It’s time for another ground-breaking, earth-shaking plan that will fix every single problem in her entire life. She then half-commits to this plan, and then one day later comes to a terrible realization....

Cindy notices that this kind of planning loop stops her from making any actual progress. It’s like she’s in a car and wants to go in a certain direction, but instead she goes into a hard right turn, and then a hard left turn, and then a hard right turn, and then a hard... you get the idea. If Cindy just stuck with a plan, even if it was kind of mediocre, then she would be able to make some sort of progress over time. It’s similar to how a random walk has an expected displacement of zero, but a directed random walk has an expected displacement that grows like n, where n is the number of steps.

Since Cindy notices that she reliably gets the extremely strong urge to stop literally everything she’s doing and make a Plan to Rule All Plans when she feels very anxious, it would be a good idea for Cindy to ban herself from planning when she feels this way—to make a deontological bar[1] against planning when anxious. This would likely mitigate the failure mode, as Cindy only really feels the urge to stop, drop, and re-plan when she’s very anxious, and really not otherwise.

Another way of saying this is that Cindy realized that she’s invariably stupid in this particular way when she’s super anxious, and so she bans herself from making decisions during this time.

II.

Tom, like many members of technical staff at frontier labs, is highly stressed when he comes home from work. Tom pretty frequently takes this out on either himself or his partner. He takes it out on himself by binge eating food, and takes it out on his partner by (somewhat unintentionally) being cold, snippy, and short with her.

In the moment, this of course feels justified on his end. Those donuts aren’t going to eat themselves. Tom is, after all, a researcher on the pretraining team, and so he uses his brain all day; chess players have to consume lots of calories during chess tournaments to fuel their mental energy expenditure—the same probably applies to pretraining research, right? This thought, and many others, is one of the concomitant lines of justification that Tom’s +3SD-IQ brain cooks up when he’s hungry and wants to post hoc justify his strong urge to eat terrible food—food that he unfailingly regrets eating afterward.

Similarly, in the moment, it feels correct to be rude to his partner. She asked him a dumb question, and he gave an answer that is already more graceful than should be expected of him. It’s not his fault that she can’t act like the other pretraining researchers and “just get it” the first time. But yet, after Tom eats his nightly DoorDashed Mexican food, he can’t help but feel bad for how he acted when he walked through the door. She’s not a frontier AI researcher—of course she doesn’t know the persnickety details of what he’s doing during the day. Tom ends up apologizing whenever this happens, and resolves for it to not happen again. But yet, it reliably does happen when he comes home.

It would be useful here for Tom to recognize when he’s stupid, and place a deontological bar against taking certain actions during this time. Tom reliably eats poor-quality food and is rude to his partner when he gets home. So Tom decides to place the rule that he (a) can’t eat any junk food until after dinner, and (b) has to be Jesus-levels of kind to his partner before eating dinner. This is because through empirical experience, if Tom leaves the decision to the moment when he’s stupid, he’ll make the wrong one. So he takes away the decision-making power from himself until he’s out of his stupidity.

III.

Claire is a normal human being with a strong imagination. Maybe she also leans anxious, but it’s not really noticeable during the day. But Claire has the funny recurring experience of waking up in the middle of the night feeling super anxious, or feeling like something could go horribly wrong at any moment. This often causes her serious fear and anxiety, and sometimes it causes her to take certain actions, like check her phone, turn the lights on to scan the room, and carefully craft a salt ring around her bed to prevent any Catholic demons from getting her. Whenever she finally gets back to sleep and wakes up the next morning, she thinks back to how she acted during the night and morbidly laughs at how stupid her actions were. She thinks of the same things that brought her anxiety at 2am, and is completely unaffected by them.

It would serve Claire well to realize when she’s stupid, and bar herself from taking any remedial actions during this time. She has empirically found that she makes downright irrational decisions during the short time period after waking up, and so she bars herself from doing anything but ignoring her scary or anxious thoughts and going back to bed. She accepts the fact that she might come across a false negative—maybe her anxious thoughts about whether or not her parents were ok combined with her 0.7% credence that ESP is real were really telling her something that one time. But probably not.

So, Claire places a deontological bar on making any decisions during this time—she pre-makes the decision when she’s smart for the times where she’s stupid.

IV.

(non-fictional example)

Bryan Johnson—the most measured man on the planet—used to consistently binge-eat every night after getting back from building Braintree Venmo. Bryan was obviously a hyper-competent individual: extremely hard-working and intelligent, with focus so sharp you could cut diamonds with it. But during the hours of 5-10pm, “Evening Bryan” took over. Evening Bryan was stressed from the day, didn’t get great sleep the night before, had multiple young kids, and also had extreme depression. (Well, Work Bryan also had all of these—but Work Bryan was occupied with work, so he didn’t really have the chance to do something like this.) Evening Bryan was a caged animal, and an entire pan of Betty Crocker Chocolate Fudge brownies was his freedom. Bryan would always binge eat tremendous amounts of food regardless of what the better-meaning Bryans wanted him to do.

So Bryan placed a deontological bar against eating during the hours of 5-10pm. Evening Bryan would valiantly protest against this dictatorial ordinance, but it worked. He stopped binge-eating, and Bryan actually credits this as one of the first steps he took toward his current Blueprint lifestyle.

V.

Around 3200 years ago, when Odysseus crossed the Tyrrhenian Sea off the coast of Southern Italy, he knew that he had to sail past the Sirens that lived on the rocks in those waters. The Sirens were known for their song—a song that compelled all men who listened to it to claw their way off of the boat and dive into the water, swimming directly into the arms of the topless bird women singing that wondrous melody. These men were then inevitably killed by these topless bird women singing that wondrous melody. But the song sure was pretty.

Knowing this devilish information, Circe instructed Odysseus to stuff his sailors’ ears with wax, thus blocking the Sirens’ song from piercing their minds.

But Odysseus wanted more.

Odysseus wanted to hear the song himself. But he knew that upon hearing their sublime song, he would surely jump to his death. So Odysseus decided to bar himself from making a decision at this time by lashing himself to the mast of his black Achaean ship. In other words, Odysseus realized when he was going to be stupid, and then placed a deontological bar on making decisions during that time.

VI.

Will Lancer[2] is highly disagreeable, confident, and has strong opinions. He also considers himself pretty fair, in the sense that he will make sure to pass an Ideological Turing Test for his opponent's position before critiquing it. But even with this internal evaluation of fairness, he reliably finds that when he encounters a new view, he will frequently form very strong opinions about it extremely quickly. These opinions will usually be to the tune of “This view is completely and utterly insane, and it is mind-blowing to me that anyone rational holds it”. He will then propagate his views in a normal manner by telling others about them in-person and online.

But Will reliably finds that, after further inspection of these positions, they were actually stronger than he gave them credit for. Maybe they aren’t something he fully agrees with, but there are serious arguments for the position. For example, Will could imagine that if he had slightly different intuitive credences on a few key premises weighing on the issue, then he would believe the viewpoint he once thought was ludicrous.

So it would probably be useful for Will to bar himself from speaking harsh words about something unless he has rigorously investigated the opposing viewpoint, say, to the point of being able to write an essay on why it’s correct. Will realizes that he’s frequently wrong and stupid when the combination of relative ignorance + extreme dismissiveness arises in response to an idea, and so he shouldn’t speak with confidence about an issue before thoroughly steelmanning[3] the opposing side.[4]

We’ve seen a lot of instances where someone realizes that they predictably make bad decisions when they’re in a certain headspace, and so this person bars themselves from taking certain actions during this time. This bar can be on specific things, like eating food, or it can be a universal bar on decision-making in general, with a pre-filled decision made ahead of time (like Claire with her post-wake anxiety and fear).

In Googling around for this post, I found that this practice actually already has a neat name: a Ulysses contract. According to Wikipedia, a Ulysses contract is a “freely made decision that is designed and intended to bind oneself in the future.” Interestingly, its name is derived from Example V above—of Odysseus (Ulysses) strapping himself to the mast, thus making a binding choice to restrict himself in the future.

The key difference between a Ulysses contract and a good ol’ fashioned resolution is the strictness of it. You should think of your future self as a caged animal that will fight with its dying breath to get what it wants in the moment—the only way to fight a creature that has just as much intelligence as you, that’s just as good at arguing as you are, and that knows all of the rationality tricks you do is to just not fight it in the first place. Get rid of your ability to make a decision in the moment rather than imploring yourself to situationally make the correct one.

If you find yourself reliably making the same bad decisions at a certain time or while you’re in a certain headspace, consider making a Ulysses contract with yourself to avoid the temptation of the Sirens.

  1. ^

    If you haven’t seen this term before, a deontological bar is simply a rule that says that it’s never ok to do something, regardless of the reasons you might have to do it. For example, Catholicism has a deontological bar against masturbation. Masturbation is always wrong, even if not masturbating meant that e.g. an infinite number of people were to be tortured for an infinite amount of time. Similarly, lying is a deontological bar in Catholicism. The Capuchin friar Padre Pio is quoted saying that “If I could end this war with a single lie, I would not tell it.” The war he’s referring to is WWII.

  2. ^

    No relation to the author whatsoever.

  3. ^

    Unlike Eliezer, I do believe in the process of steelmanning. The reason I consider the Ideological Turing Test insufficient is because it’s too easy to fool yourself with it—at least, it was for me. I would articulate the position I disagreed with to a defender of that position, they would agree with it, I would point out fifteen errors with what they believe, and I would walk away vindicated in my belief. But that’s really not the standard you want to shoot for. Especially if you’re good at debating or thinking about things, I would strongly recommend making the best case possible for the opposing side using all of that brainpower you have. The truth of the matter is that you are frequently the strongest intellectual opponent you have immediate access to, and using those abilities for the opposing side is good intellectual practice. As a side note, I consider steelmanning your opponent to be an application of Jesus’ dictum of loving your enemies. I will probably write a blog post later about the virtues of steelmanning in general, as well as its virtues as opposed to passing an Ideological Turing Test.

  4. ^

    Guys, I have something to admit to you. This “Will Lancer” character in the story, the one that I told you wasn’t me? Yeah. About that.... On the bright side, I’m finding that truly steelmanning the opposing side is both fun and epistemically helpful for finding flaws in my thinking. And I only really started doing this in response to the idea that I’m writing about right now!

In that spirit, I notice The Great AI Hackening is at least as imminent as covid was in January 2020, maybe closer. What specific things should people do to personally prepare? What are your unresolved cruxes that would let you answer that question?
